claims.text: Preferential surface segregation of Cu governs the onset of melting in FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles.
Cu has the lowest melting point among Fe, Ni, Cr, Co, and Cu.
Cu surface segregation reduces the local cohesive energy at the nanoparticle surface.
Surface segregation produces a Cu-enriched liquid-like layer.
The Cu-enriched layer triggers progression to complete melting after reaching a critical thickness.
The starting nanoparticles are homogeneous crystalline FeNiCrCoCu solid solutions with uniform elemental distributions.
At elevated temperature, Cu atoms diffuse toward and accumulate at the nanoparticle surface because of surface-energy effects.
Localized Cu enrichment lowers the local melting temperature.
A sufficiently thick liquid-like surface layer destabilizes the underlying solid matrix and propagates inward.
A Cu-rich surface region will appear before complete melting.
The emerging surface region will exhibit liquid-like atomic mobility and morphological rounding.
The liquid-like surface layer will thicken with increasing temperature and eventually merge with the particle interior.
Complete melting will culminate in a homogeneous molten state.
The proposed surface-driven mechanism should dominate in particles below approximately 20 nm because of their high surface-to-volume ratio.
Larger particles or particles with modified surface chemistry may exhibit different melting behavior.
The critical temperature and extent of Cu segregation may vary with particle size, crystallographic orientation, and local defects.
